articles.title: Did Neuralink make the wrong bet?
articles.summary: The field of brain-computer interfaces is moving away from mind-controlled computer cursors to restoring speech.
articles.body: Elon Musk promised Neuralink would bring superhuman abilities and minds merged with AI. Then he fueled a runaway hype train for his brain implant technology, which ended up with a grisly record for implants in monkeys and some success with human subjects. But for all of the hype, he’s still further away than Mars from his goal. And that’s because his relentless ambition is once again hitting the wall of scientific reality. The heart of the issue is how brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) translate thought into results. Neuralink’s products have all been brain-to-cursor interfaces, which allow patients to control a mouse with their minds. But Neuralink’s competitors have raced ahead with newer BCIs that translate thought directly to speech. Turns out that’s a more promising approach — enough to convince Neuralink to quietly invest in BCIs that focus on speech. Musk has a strong record of overpromising and underdelivering, and his biggest quagmire may end up being his pursuit of a grand, unified vision of a human-AI-hybrid technology. When it comes to the human mind, he’s underestimated and oversimplified the steps it will take to make meaningful brain-computer interfaces a reality for patients who really need them. BCIs are similar, but there’s a big difference All BCIs connect a brain to a computer with wires or Bluetooth. They stalk the tiny bursts of electricity your neurons use to talk to each other and then try to make sense of them so that they can predict what you might want to do in the future. The key difference between BCIs is the type of behavior they’re trying to emulate. A motor BCI, like the one Neuralink has been building, helps users guide a cursor across a computer screen. Unlike those, speech BCIs translate brain waves into sounds and small sections of words called phonemes. In the span of five years, speech BCIs have reached impressive milestones that rival the achievements of the two-decade-old motor BCI technology. A 2019 study reported that a speech BCI could predict what a person planned to say when given only a few options. By 2024, a 45-year-old ALS patient could speak naturally with 97 percent accuracy using his speech BCI. In November 2025, Neuralink patient Brad Smith showed The Verge his motor BCI. He thought about moving his arm, which he could no longer move due to ALS, and instead the computer cursor moved across the screen. For speech BCIs, it’s words or chunks of words. Patients think about speaking the word “good,” for example, and the word appears on the screen. It is not mind reading — it is detecting what they’re trying to say. Here is the catch: Both versions are technically motor BCIs. The underlying neuroscience is the same. If you move your finger, your brain is sending signals down into the muscles in your pinky. If you talk, your brain sends similar signals down into your tongue and other muscles that help you form sounds. The BCI detects what muscle the user is thinking about moving, whether tongue or finger, and predicts what they’re trying to do or say. A pivot forward Neuralink is now course-correcting to be in line with the rest of the BCI community: In May, Neuralink began recruiting patients for a clinical trial to study speech restoration at the Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi hospital in the United Arab Emirates; in October, it launched a speech restoration trial in the United States at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center. The patients will use the same hardware as the current Neuralink patients but for the goal of turning their thoughts into speech rather than cursor movements. The company has already claimed success in a video posted to X on March 24th of a speech BCI trial participant who can still speak but whose speech is hard to understand because of ALS. Speech BCIs seem to be the future of the field, but it remains to be seen whether the technology will speed past motor BCIs to market or simply offer another technology option to patients with different needs. Neuralink has been making moves to step into its commercial era. The company hired a former director of the FDA office that oversees medical devices like BCIs to head its medical affairs, and Musk announced that Neuralink will begin “high-volume production” of the devices in a post on X on December 31st, though any Musk production predictions need to be taken with a grain of salt. As Musk’s medical company falls in line with the broader BCI field, does it also drift further from his vision of human enhancement and back to regular medical assistance for those who need it most? It is unclear. Space is hard; the brain is harder Sergey Stavisky was one half of the leadership team for the 2024 speech BCI research study out of the University of California, Davis that set a high bar for speech BCI accuracy. Stavisky was a former motor BCI researcher but pivoted to speech BCI in 2019 to make rapid progress in a field that looked to him ripe for success. “It seemed like it was a bit of an untapped opportunity,” he said. This has borne out, he said, noting how speech BCIs quickly expanded the size of their vocabulary from only 50 words to “being able to say any word in the dictionary,” he said. But he doesn’t think that Neuralink made the wrong bet to focus on motor BCIs when the company formed in 2016. At that time, academic research into motor BCIs had matured enough for industry to step in, he said. “I think at that time, cursor control was sufficiently de-risked by academic trials that it was clear that with better hardware, a very useful medical device could be built,” he said. (Stavisky has been a paid consultant for Neuralink in the past, but he did not provide details because he signed a non-disclosure agreement. It is not uncommon for academic BCI researchers to consult with for-profit BCI companies. Stavisky is tangentially working with Neuralink’s competitor Paradromics on its upcoming clinical trial through his coinvestigator at Davis.) Matt Angle, CEO of Paradromics, disagrees. Neuralink did make a mistake by focusing on motor BCIs, he told The Verge. Paradromics started one year earlier, in 2015, with speech as its first priority. Like Stavisky, many top Paradromics scientists come from the motor BCI research field. Speech is a better first application of BCI technology than motor restoration, from Angle’s perspective, because it’s “the biggest quality-of-life deltas that you can imagine,” he said, “being able to talk to your loved ones again — and it’s something that BCI can do today.” I asked Angle why a motor BCI might not be as valuable to a patient unable to talk as a speech BCI given that both result in words spoken aloud by a computer program. I witnessed Neuralink patient Brad Smith use his motor BCI to communicate in a real-time conversation with me and his wife in November. Smith typed out answers to my questions letter by letter, word by word, with his mind-controlled computer cursor. Smith told me that Neuralink changed his life for the better. Speed limits motor BCIs, according to Angle. (Smith typed out his 16-word response to my question in one minute and 17 seconds.) “If I lost the ability to communicate and my primary means of communication was the BCI, I would like to have speech back,” he said. Still, he is quick to note that all BCIs, speech and motor, should exist: “I don’t think it’s for us to armchair what someone with a disability would or wouldn’t want,” Angle said. Looking further, AI chatbots seem like an obvious complement to speech BCIs. The two technologies are tangentially related: BCIs are already built on algorithms similar to the large language models powering AI chatbots, and many people with speech impairments use predictive word software — again, somewhat related to LLMs — to pick out which words or phrases they most likely want to say next. (Smith used text-to-speech app Proloquo4Text in conjunction with his Neuralink BCI.) Speech BCIs could make it easier and faster, with fewer clicks, to input prompts into AI chatbots, and access the benefits of agents and agentic browsers (when they work) to navigate the virtual world. Patients want all types of BCIs Former BCI user Ian Burkhart was unable to speak or move during the two weeks following a diving accident in 2010 that resulted in a spinal cord injury. Communication emerged as “a huge, huge priority” during that time, more so than being able to move, he said. Burkhart now appears to speak with relative ease and has recovered partial movement of his hands. But he said he would still like a speech BCI today, just for the ability to rapidly input text into a computer. This seems noteworthy given that Burkhart is one of the several dozen people in the world to actually use a motor BCI. He was part of a roughly seven-year-long clinical trial at The Ohio State University, where he controlled a computer cursor and played Guitar Hero with this brain. He also became the first person to reanimate some muscles in his body using electrical stimulators controlled by his thoughts. If forced to choose between speech or motor BCIs, ALS patient Spero Koulouras told The Verge in a written comment: “for me it’s motor by a mile.” A former software engineer and entrepreneur, Koulouras says that he is “effectively quadriplegic and mute” over six years after his diagnosis with ALS in 2019. He communicates entirely through his computer and spends much of his day writing code and doing 3D design, all of which contribute to his preference for a mind-controlled computer cursor rather than a brain-to-speech BCI. Both technologies come with downsides, Koulouras noted. Speech BCIs cannot enable him “to be fully functional in [his] virtual environment,” he said. “But family gatherings are torturous,” he said, even though he uses prerecorded phrases to make a point within a conversation. “The inability to joke, snark, and harass friends and relatives in real time is emotionally devastating… Motor control today can’t provide the communication speed to be an active participant.” Koulouras was not selected to join Neuralink’s motor BCI trial after the company evaluated him in February 2025. He is not sure why but guesses that his existing technology works well — too well, perhaps. He uses a motion tracker device called Cato that attaches to his glasses and translates subtle head movements into cursor movements on a screen. Koulouras is the cofounder of the company behind the device, Auli.Tech. “I believe my proficiency with my current tech may have factored into Neuralink’s decision. As a clinical trial I may not have had as much potential for improvement, negatively impacting reported results,” he said. In June 2025, Neuralink contacted him again for its speech BCI trial, but his low respiratory scores would have required him to get a tracheostomy, which he declined. Koulouras’ experience highlights just how inaccessible BCI technology is for most patients. Potential BCI users need to meet a long list of criteria to be considered for a trial, after meeting the most obvious criterion of simply living near a trial location. Advocacy groups the ALS Association and the ALS Network, which connected Spero to The Verge, include information or host events about BCIs on their websites, but the bulk of their efforts are focused on advocating for insurance reimbursement for necessities like wheelchairs, navigating healthcare denials, and increased research funding. “From a cursor guided by thought to speech restored directly from the mind, every advance in brain–computer interfaces represents real progress for real people,” ALS Network president and CEO Sheri Strahl wrote to The Verge. “Each breakthrough - whether restoring movement, communication, or autonomy - expands dignity and quality of life. It all matters, and it’s encouraging to see so many innovative scientists taking different approaches toward the same deeply human goal.” “What’s the market?” There is the question of what patients want, and there is another question of how many patients might benefit from it. In other words, “What’s the market?” associate professor Kip Ludwig asked when speaking to The Verge. Ludwig leads an institute focused on neuroengineering at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where he studies how electrical zaps to the body’s nerves can treat heart failure and other complex disorders. For all BCIs, “it’s incredibly small for an incredibly expensive technology,” he said. Most motor BCI patients have either ALS or a paralysis from a spinal cord injury. There are roughly 30,000 ALS patients and 300,000 patients with traumatic spinal cord injury in the US, according to recent estimates. In order to enter a BCI clinical trial, participants must also live within a several-hour drive of the trial site, have a caregiver who can assist them, and not have other serious medical conditions like epilepsy or anything requiring regular MRIs. Motor BCI companies, therefore, have to find other patient populations that might benefit from their technology. Stroke patients with a less severe motor dysfunction than full quadriplegia are an obvious target population. But, if the spinal cord is doing its job and sending signals from the brain and out to the nerves, then these same patients don’t really need a brain surgery, Ludwig argued. Motor BCIs are “an invasive version of something I can do less invasively in the periphery,” he said. Speech BCIs, in contrast, might be a good fit for stroke patients, according to Paradromics CEO Angle. The company is first focusing on a small group of patients with ALS or an injury that affects muscles or nerves. As the trials of speech BCIs located in the motor cortex progress, Angle said the company plans to launch more clinical trials in other parts of the brain, like the superior temporal gyrus, which has been shown to encode spoken speech and internal speech, like an inner monologue. Tapping into the STG can open up the patient pool to those with strokes in the motor region of their brain, and who can no longer speak. After these small feasibility studies show that speech BCIs are safe, like all clinical trials, later studies will include more and more patients so that enough data can convince the FDA that the tech is so useful that it should come to market. The reality of augmentation Perhaps the largest divide within the BCI industry is not speech versus motor, but augmentation versus medical assistance. At the company’s 2019 launch event, Musk set Neuralink’s ultimate goal as a “full brain-machine interface,” which he defined as “a sort of symbiosis with artificial intelligence.” Motor BCIs were the necessary stepping stones to his eventual goal of augmenting any human who wants a BCI to achieve superhuman AI incorporation. Neuralink first needed to “solve” several “issues” related to “brain disorders” like Alzheimer’s or dementia, as well as paralysis resulting from broken or injured spines. But the theory behind augmentation has a major flaw: Evolution capped how much information can flow from the brain to the body, associate professor at University of Wisconsin-Madison Kip Ludwig told The Verge. “In reality, we’re limited by our own physiology,” he said. Even if BCIs got super fast at decoding the brain’s signals, we would not be able to make the most of it, he said. “Evolution did a great job.” “There’s this false assumption that they can get so good at brain-machine interfaces that they can decode from the brain faster than we can encode with our natural body typing or swinging a baseball bat or things like that,” Ludwig said. He is quite familiar with the “natural rate” of information transfer — he measures the brain-to-organ latency rate as part of his own research exploring the ways that electrical zaps to the body’s nerves can treat complex disorders like heart failure. Motor BCIs could, in theory, shave 200 milliseconds or so off someone’s reaction time, he said. That is roughly how long it takes for a command from the brain to travel down nerves into muscles and cause a movement. But that isn’t that useful to people trying to regain independence in doing tasks at home, he said. For now, speech BCIs don’t seem to fit into the futuristic vision of human augmentation, Ludwig noted. It could get more sci-fi if the technology moves from motor regions of the brain that control the mouth to areas that tap into abstract ideas of language — and could decode someone’s inner monologue. The “bummer” of commercial BCI efforts Technical success does not necessarily translate into commercial success, as seen by the boom-and-bust cycles of many medical device companies attempting experimental technologies. A pair of companies providing retinal prostheses to partially blind patients offer two unrelated examples. Both Second Sight Medical and Pixium Vision went bankrupt and left patients stranded with unserviceable technology; both also had their IP bought, and their patients rescued, by newer medtech ventures, one of whom was Science Corporation, founded by Neuralink cofounder Max Hodak. Blackrock Neurotech may boast over 19 years of testing in humans, but the company has pushed back the year that it expects to commercialize its at-home motor BCI system called MoveAgain. In 2021, the company predicted that it could bring MoveAgain to market within the year. In 2022, I spoke to the company’s cofounder and then-president, now chief science officer, Florian Solzbacher for STAT News. Only one document required by the FDA stood between the company and its commercialization goal of 2023. “We are quite confident that this will work,” Solzbacher said at the time. But the deadline came and went. In 2024, when the investment arm of crypto company Tether took a majority stake in Blackrock Neurotech, the announcement lacked mention of a timeline for commercialization. Blackrock Neurotech did not respond to The Verge’s multiple requests for comment on the commercialization delay. “It’s a bummer,” Burkhart said of the delay. While he occasionally consults with Blackrock Neurotech, he can only surmise the reason for the delay. Medical insurance reimbursement tops his list. Home devices are always a pain to get reimbursed by insurance companies, which disabled people know all too well. Motor BCIs are a particularly unique device with no precedent, he said. “There’s no medical justification that says people need to be able to use a computer or use a robotic arm or use a muscle stimulation device, anything like that,” he said. Speech, in contrast, does have precedent. “But there is medical justification for people being able to accurately convey their health needs,” he adds. The vast number of speech generators or alternative communication devices already FDA-approved and reimbursable by insurance might make the reimbursement pathway for speech BCIs a “little bit cleaner” compared to motor BCIs, he said. As of June 2025, Neuralink has implanted between five and 12 humans — reports vary and Neuralink did not respond to our requests for an exact count — since the first patient was implanted in January 2024. While impressive, Neuralink trails Blackrock Neurotech’s 52 total patients by several dozen. It remains to be seen whether speech BCIs can leap-frog traditional cursor-based motor BCIs to the commercial market. Motor BCIs have the advantage of patient use at home, which the FDA will use to evaluate the safety of the technology. Speech BCIs, meanwhile, have only been used in controlled lab settings. And yet, Angle is unconcerned about which type of BCIs will come to market first. He is convinced that whenever patients have the option to speak again with a speech BCI, they’ll choose to get the device. It’s the adoption of the technology that matters more to him. “It’s about making sure that we’re launching not a gee-whiz gadget but an actual medical device that meets an important unmet medical need and is delivering value to the people who get it.”

articles.title: In Mexico's Los Tuxtlas rainforest, where about 60% of original tree cover is gone, scientists found endangered howler monkeys carry signs of habitat damage in their gut bacteria, not just their surroundings
articles.summary: It is widely believed that we are what we eat, a phrase that can now extend to an endangered species as well.
articles.body: It is widely believed that we are what we eat, a phrase that can now extend to an endangered species as well. With the loss of habitat, not only can an entire species be put at risk of extinction through the loss of shelter and food, but its body can also experience significant changes. These effects can extend beyond the landscape itself, as scientists are now finding clues to habitat damage in an unexpected place: the gut of an animal.According to a Northwestern University report, scientists from both the Northwestern University and Universidad Veracruzana studying endangered Mexican mantled howler monkeys in the Los Tuxtlas Biosphere Reserve in Veracruz, Mexico, ascertained that differences in their forest habitats and the environmental changes have come to alter and reflect in a howler monkey’s gut microbiomes.The findings were published in the journal Animal Conservation on November 15, 2026, under the title Multi-Biomarker Fecal Assessment of Habitat Disturbance Effects in an Endangered Howler Monkey. Led by Tabor L. Whitney, the study explored how habitat fragmentation and changes in vegetation were associated with different biological indicators in the endangered subspecies.A rainforest losing its original coverThe research was conducted in the Los Tuxtlas Biosphere Reserve, an area that has undergone considerable environmental change over the last few years. As reported in the study, nearly 60% of its original forest cover is gone, leaving behind a landscape made up of human settlements, agricultural fields and pastures interspersed with smaller patches of forest. These remaining parts have served as crucial spaces for wildlife to continue surviving, especially the Mexican mantled howler monkey (Alouatta palliata mexicana), a testament to its resilience in deteriorating environmental conditions.For animals that depend on trees for food and movement, the loss of a continuous forest canopy can make everyday activities more difficult. Fewer tree species can also mean fewer dietary options, while isolated patches may restrict the movement of animals between different parts of the forest. The researchers therefore aimed to understand why these changes are reflected in the monkeys' physiology.What the researchers found in their gut bacteriaThe team studied howler monkeys living across 10 forest fragments that differed in size, tree diversity, vegetation structure and connectivity. They collected faecal samples from the animals and examined three different biological indicators: gut microbiome composition, short-chain fatty acids and glucocorticoid metabolites.The gut microbiome essentially refers to the community of microorganisms, including bacteria, living in the digestive system. These microorganisms are important for several bodily functions, including the digestion of food, energy metabolism and immune regulation. In animals that consume plant material, gut bacteria also help break down dietary fibres that the digestive system would otherwise struggle to process. To put it simply, the condition of a forest can influence not only what an animal eats but also the microorganisms that help it process that food.The study found significant differences in gut microbiome diversity and composition between the 10 forest fragments. The size of a forest patch, the diversity of its tree species, the average diameter of its trees and the number of tree lines connecting different areas were among the characteristics associated with these variations. However, a difference was noted in how monkeys living in smaller forest fragments with smaller trees and lower tree diversity had substantially different gut microbiome compositions from those in more mature forest habitats.Another key difference highlighted in the research related to the abundance of certain bacterial groups across habitats. For instance, some bacteria associated with breaking down plant fibres were more strongly associated with larger trees and better-connected forest areas. However, the researchers cautioned that these bacterial functions were inferred from existing knowledge about the identified microorganisms and were not directly tested.Looking beyond the gut microbiomeThe researchers did not limit their investigation to gut bacteria. They also examined short-chain fatty acids, which are produced when gut microorganisms ferment dietary fibres, and glucocorticoid metabolites, which are hormones measured in faeces and can provide information about an animal's physiological stress responses.These additional indicators helped the team understand whether the changes observed in the microbiome were accompanied by other physiological differences. Interestingly, the results were not identical across all three measurements. While gut microbiome composition differed significantly between forest fragments, short-chain fatty acid concentrations did not show significant differences between the locations. Glucocorticoid concentrations also showed no statistically significant variation between fragments, although some relationships with individual habitat characteristics were observed.The research, however, exclusively focused on adult male howler monkeys, with the scientists explaining that the available hormonal testing method had been biologically validated for this particular group. The results therefore cannot automatically be extended to females or younger monkeys, whose physiological and dietary requirements may differ.A look at the future of conservationTraditionally, monitoring endangered animals involves observing population numbers, mapping their habitats and assessing changes in the availability of food and shelter. While these remain essential, the study suggests that examining faecal samples could provide another way of understanding how animals are responding to environmental changes.Lead author Tabor Whitney also suggested that researchers could collect samples every five or 10 years to compare changes in gut microbiomes and evaluate whether conservation efforts are making a difference. According to the Northwestern University report, landowners in the region have also expressed interest in helping monkeys move between forest areas by maintaining tree connections on their properties.The study concludes that there may be practical approaches that can be adopted to improve the remaining forest areas, such as planting a greater variety of trees, especially fruit-bearing species that can provide an abundance of food for monkeys and birds. Lastly, expanding the forest canopy and creating connected lines of trees, even across isolated patches, can make it easier for monkeys to move between habitats and forage for food.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk watches the birth of daughter Katherine Grace from the International Space Station; her name honours the capsule that carried him to orbit
articles.summary: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk watched the birth of his daughter, Katherine Grace, from the International Space Station on Tuesday 24 November 2026, as
articles.body: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk watched the birth of his daughter, Katherine Grace, from the International Space Station on Tuesday 24 November 2026, as his wife, Heather, gave birth to their third child in Houston. The baby's name honours Grace, the SpaceX capsule that carried him and his crewmates to orbit on 1 October. Kutryk, 44, a Canadian Space Agency astronaut, was eight weeks into a six-month stay, circling Earth about 250 miles up. The orbiting laboratory, roughly the size of a football field, completes a lap about every 90 minutes. The couple's two older children are aged 7 and 5.Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk shares birth of his daughter from the International Space StationAccording to CBS News, the Canadian Space Agency said in a news release that Heather and the baby were both doing well and that Joshua Kutryk was able to share in the experience from the space station. In a joint statement, the couple said Kutryk is living out a childhood dream aboard the station and that, despite the distance, they feel incredibly connected as they welcome their new little star. The report described him as only the fourth astronaut to miss the birth of a child, and the 17th Canadian to fly in space.ID@undefined Caption not available.Why daughter Katherine Grace's name honours the SpaceX capsule that carried Joshua Kutryk to orbitAccording to Today, SpaceX names each capsule that ferries astronauts to space, much as ships are named, which gives the baby's name its link to his journey. Today described the birth as Heather's own mission, calling it "a big launch of her own".Joshua Kutryk's first spaceflight: Crew 13 launch, public service and a newborn daughterKutryk, a former military test pilot, launched from Florida on 1 October aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule as part of Crew 13, alongside two astronauts from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration and a Russian cosmonaut. It is his first spaceflight.Before departure, Kutryk told CBS News that missing the birth would be hard, but that he would try to take the positive things out of it. He added that he hoped his new child would see the mission as taking some sacrifice and risk in the name of public service for Canada. As of 24 November, Crew 13 had no confirmed date for its return to Earth.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Archaeologists digging ahead of an electricity substation in western Hungary found more than 200 Celtic silver coins packed in a small clay pot 40cm underground, the largest such hoard there in over 50 years
articles.summary: One person's construction site can be another archaeologist's treasure trove!
articles.body: One person's construction site can be another archaeologist's treasure trove! What was supposed to make way for a new electricity substation in Szombathely, Hungary, has now led to a remarkable discovery.More than 200 Celtic silver coins, some of which had been preserved inside a small clay pot, were found buried just 30 to 40 centimetres (approximately 12 to 16 inches) beneath the ground. What began as an archaeological investigation ahead of the construction project eventually led researchers to uncover a hoard that had remained hidden for more than 2,000 years.E.ON, the Hungarian energy company, recently announced the discovery in an official statement, with the findings also reported by Live Science. The coins, which weigh more than two kilograms (approximately 4.4 pounds), constitute the largest such hoard discovered in Hungary in over 50 years. According to Eszter Kreiter, an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Institute, the last comparable discovery in the country was made in the late 1960s.While the silver coins are the most remarkable find at the centre of the discovery, they are not all that archaeologists came across. The excavation also revealed a brick bearing the footprint of a Roman-era dog, unusual jewellery, prehistoric tools and several other objects that offer a glimpse into the lives of communities that occupied the area thousands of years ago.The archaeological findingsThe team of archaeologists was already aware that the proposed construction site was of archaeological importance. Therefore, excavations were carried out between 2023 and 2025 by specialists from the National Archaeological Institute of the Hungarian National Museum Public Collections Centre. The site required archaeological investigations before and alongside the construction-related earthworks.The archaeological work eventually uncovered nearly 400 archaeological features and several thousand artefacts, with evidence of human activity dating from the fifth millennium BC through to the early modern period.The oldest discoveries included a polished stone tool dating back almost 7,000 years, which was likely used for woodworking. Archaeologists also found a glass bead decorated with a peacock-eye pattern, believed to have been part of jewellery from around the seventh or sixth century BC. Vessels that may have been used to contain food and drink were also discovered alongside burials.Among the other discoveries were two well-preserved stones from a hand-operated mill, found inside a semi-subterranean building dating to the Celtic period.The site also contained evidence of a Roman-era villa estate. Although the original building had been dismantled over the centuries, archaeologists were able to partially reconstruct its layout, including its underfloor heating system. One particularly unusual discovery was a fragment of brick bearing the imprint of a dog's paw, believed to have been left when the clay was still soft. The brick may once have been used in the construction of the villa's heating system.About the Celtic coinsThe silver hoard consists of more than 200 coins identified as Velem-type tetradrachms. These coins date from the late second century BC to the early first century BC and were buried in a pit approximately 30–40 centimetres beneath the ground. While some of the coins had been placed inside a small ceramic vessel, agricultural activity over the centuries had disturbed the deposit.According to Live Science, the coins are worth more than $2,000 in today's market based on their silver content alone. However, their historical and archaeological significance makes them considerably more valuable than the price of the metal they contain.The coins are modelled on Greek tetradrachms, an early form of large silver currency introduced in the late sixth century BC. The Velem type takes its name from Velem-Szent Vid, a fortified Celtic hilltop settlement, or oppidum, located approximately 15 kilometres west of the excavation site. Similar coins have previously been discovered there.Each coin features a stylised head on one side, believed to represent the Greek god Apollo, while the other side depicts a helmeted rider on a horse. These designs reflect the influence of Greek coinage on Celtic communities, which adapted existing designs to develop their own forms of currency.The history and significance of Celtic coinageBut what do we really know about the Celtic communities and their use of coinage?Some research studies have suggested that Celtic coin production in the region could have begun around the middle of the third century BC, with some of the earliest coins modelled on the silver tetradrachms of Philip II of Macedon. Their designs reflected the influence of Greek currency, although Celtic communities gradually developed distinctive imagery of their own. The purpose of these large silver coins, however, has continued to remain a subject of scholarly discussion.While the precise reason behind the burial of the Szombathely hoard remains unknown, the discovery could open up new avenues of research into the history of Celtic communities and their use of silver currency.According to E.ON's official statement, the discoveries made during the excavation will soon be presented to the public in a temporary exhibition at the Savaria Museum in Szombathely.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Neuralink has received FDA approval for a new trial on ALS patients.
articles.summary:

articles.title: Why do some children struggle with attention, anxiety or both? Stanford researchers used AI to identify three distinct brain patterns that may help explain why children experience these conditions differently
articles.summary: Children diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and anxiety may display similar symptoms, but the underlying brain patterns
articles.body: Children diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and anxiety may display similar symptoms, but the underlying brain patterns associated with their difficulties could be quite different. A new study led by Stanford Medicine researchers, published in Nature Mental Health on October 16, 2026, has identified three distinct brain patterns in children with these conditions, potentially offering a new way to understand why they experience emotional and behavioural difficulties differently. The research, also reported by Stanford University and indexed by the National Library of Medicine, uses artificial intelligence to examine how different regions of the brain communicate. Its findings suggest that conventional diagnostic labels may not fully capture the biological differences between children experiencing attention problems, anxiety or a combination of both.What the researchers discoveredThe team analysed brain imaging and behavioural data from children aged 9 to 11 who were part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a large US research project tracking childhood brain development. Using an AI-powered deep-learning model, researchers examined functional connectivity, which refers to the way different parts of the brain communicate and work together. They combined these findings with cognitive assessments, behavioural information and existing diagnoses to identify patterns that might otherwise be difficult to distinguish.The analysis revealed two major dimensions of brain-behaviour difficulties: cognitive and behavioural control, and the regulation of emotions and attention. Different combinations of these patterns were associated with three distinct biotypes.Three brain patterns linked to different symptomsThe first, known as the externalising-disinhibited biotype, was associated with impulsivity, hostility, defiance, aggression and rule-breaking. Children in this group were more likely to have an ADHD diagnosis.The second, called the internalising-distressed biotype, was characterised by feelings of guilt, tension and perfectionism, alongside symptoms associated with anxiety and depression. Anxiety diagnoses were more common among children in this category. The third was the mixed biotype, which involved a combination of difficulties, including attention problems, irritability and some self-injurious behaviour. Children in this group were also more likely to have ADHD diagnoses.However, the researchers found that these patterns did not correspond exclusively to any one diagnosis. Children with ADHD, anxiety or both conditions could belong to any of the three groups. This suggests that children carrying the same clinical diagnosis may have considerably different underlying brain-behaviour profiles.Brain patterns could emerge before diagnosisOne of the more significant findings was that the researchers could identify these brain patterns in children who had not received an ADHD or anxiety diagnosis when they first entered the study but were diagnosed later. This raises the possibility that certain patterns of brain connectivity could eventually help identify children who may be at risk of developing these conditions before their symptoms become more pronounced.To test whether their findings extended beyond the original research group, the team also examined brain scans from 224 children participating in a separate project, the Healthy Brain Network. The results provided additional support for the three biotypes. The findings are particularly relevant because ADHD and anxiety frequently overlap in childhood. A child experiencing anxiety may struggle to concentrate, while a child with ADHD may also experience emotional distress. This overlap can make it difficult to understand which difficulties are driving a child’s behaviour and what kind of support might be most effective.Could this change how children are treated?The researchers believe that identifying these biological differences could eventually help clinicians develop more targeted approaches to treatment. Currently, children diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety are often assessed through their symptoms and clinical history. Finding an appropriate treatment can involve trying different medications or therapeutic approaches before identifying what works best.The new research offers a possible direction for improving this process. If future studies establish clear connections between particular brain patterns and treatment responses, clinicians could potentially use this information to make more informed decisions about individual care.However, the findings do not mean that brain scans can currently diagnose ADHD or anxiety, or that existing diagnostic methods should be replaced. The study establishes associations between brain connectivity and behavioural patterns, rather than proving that these brain differences directly cause the conditions.For now, the three biotypes offer researchers a more detailed framework for studying why children with apparently similar diagnoses can have very different experiences. Further research will be needed to establish whether these patterns can reliably guide diagnosis, predict outcomes and improve treatment.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: In 2014, former Kenyan radio host Raabia Hawa set up a ranger group on the Lamu coast, and in one stronghold the endangered coastal topi has grown from about 33 animals to more than 300, winning her a Tusk award
articles.summary: Kenyan conservationist Raabia Hawa, who left a career in radio to protect wildlife, has won the 2026 Tusk Award for Conservation in Africa for her work
articles.body: Kenyan conservationist Raabia Hawa, who left a career in radio to protect wildlife, has won the 2026 Tusk Award for Conservation in Africa for her work against poaching and environmental destruction. Her efforts have helped bring an endangered antelope population back from the brink, while also strengthening the role of local communities in protecting threatened ecosystems. According to Tusk Trust, which announced this year’s winners following its November 11 ceremony in London, Hawa was recognised for her leadership through the Ulinzi Africa Foundation, an organisation she founded in 2014. Reporting by Mongabay and Nature Africa has also highlighted her transition from broadcasting to frontline conservation and the growing scope of her environmental work. Scroll down to read more…From radio to wildlife conservationHawa’s journey into conservation began while she was working as a radio presenter in Kenya. Although she had developed an interest in wildlife from an early age, witnessing the consequences of elephant poaching and the risks faced by wildlife rangers prompted her to take a more active role. She initially used her media platform to draw attention to wildlife crime, but eventually decided that raising awareness was not enough. She wanted to work directly with the people protecting animals on the ground.That decision led to the establishment of Ulinzi Africa Foundation in 2014. The organisation initially focused on supporting rangers and strengthening anti-poaching efforts in areas where wildlife protection remained under-resourced. Over the years, its work has expanded across Kenya’s Lamu and Tana River regions, bringing together wildlife monitoring, community engagement and environmental advocacy.How coastal topi numbers recoveredOne of the most significant outcomes associated with Hawa’s conservation work has been the recovery of coastal topi in one of their remaining strongholds. According to Tusk, the population in the area increased from approximately 33 to 34 animals to more than 300. The improvement has been attributed to sustained anti-poaching patrols, habitat protection and the work of local ranger teams.The recovery is particularly significant because the coastal topi, a subspecies of antelope, has experienced a severe decline across its historical range. A 2026 report published by Ulinzi Africa Foundation, drawing on conservation research and population assessments, highlights the scale of the problem. It estimates that coastal topi numbers in Kenya fell by approximately 92 per cent between 1977 and 2013.The report also points to further declines in subsequent years, making the protection of remaining populations increasingly important. The organisation’s work is therefore not simply about preventing individual incidents of poaching. It involves protecting the habitats that allow wildlife populations to survive and reproduce.Conservation that involves local communitiesHawa’s approach also places considerable emphasis on the people who live alongside wildlife. Rangers are central to the foundation’s operations, but community participation is equally important to the long-term success of conservation initiatives. Her work has increasingly extended beyond land-based wildlife protection. As highlighted in Mongabay’s November 2026 profile, Hawa has also challenged destructive industrial fishing practices and extractive activities that threaten coastal ecosystems and local livelihoods.The conservationist has faced serious personal risks because of her work, including threats linked to her opposition to environmentally damaging activities. She has also advocated for greater participation by women in conservation, encouraging them to take up leadership and frontline roles in a field traditionally dominated by men.Recognition at the 2026 Tusk Conservation AwardsHawa received the Tusk Award for Conservation in Africa at the November 11 ceremony in London. The award recognises conservationists demonstrating exceptional leadership and making a meaningful contribution to protecting Africa’s natural heritage. She was among three individuals recognised this year. Dr Colleen Begg, whose work with the Niassa Carnivore Project in Mozambique has helped protect large carnivores across an extensive wilderness landscape, received the Prince William Award for Conservation in Africa.Meanwhile, Daniel Yiankere, security manager at Kenya’s Loisaba Conservancy, received the Tusk Wildlife Ranger Award for his contribution to wildlife protection and ranger operations. For Hawa, the recognition reflects years of work by rangers and communities operating in difficult conditions. Her story also highlights how conservation can move beyond traditional protection efforts when local leadership, sustained fieldwork and community involvement come together.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Mexico seeks US talks about suspected SpaceX debris
articles.summary: Mexico concerned as SpaceX ramps up rocket launches from Starbase near border in Texas.
articles.body:
The Mexican government is seeking talks with aviation authorities in the United States about falling rocket debris following SpaceX launches in Texas.

It is the latest sign of growing tensions between Mexico City and Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar company.

“What we are seeking, through the embassy, is a meeting between US and Mexican airspace authorities so that permission for the use of Mexican airspace can be established, how often it would be used, and, if necessary, the relocation of the launch site,” Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Thursday at a news conference in the capital.

“And then there’s the ⁠⁠⁠⁠issue of the debris,” she added.

Earlier this month, Mexican authorities said they had to recover debris after a launch of a SpaceX Starship from its Starbase,Texas, facility near the Gulf of Mexico and nature reserves on both sides of the shared border.

Debris that officials said came from the launch washed ashore along Playa Bagdad in Matamoros in the Mexican state of Tamaulipas, according to PROFEPA, Mexico’s Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection.

It said it had collected material several days after part of the Starship was destroyed and fell into the sea. The debris was taken by the Mexican navy to be stored and PROFEPA said it would ask SpaceX to take possession of it.

SpaceX said it was working with Mexican authorities and disputed the claim that what was found was from its failed Starship launch.

“We continue to stay in contact with the Mexican government and are on standby to send support if authorities in Mexico tell us it is actually needed,” the company posted on X. “Partners on the ground relayed that they have found very little debris in their sweeps of the beach and the small amount they have found is not clearly from SpaceX operations.”

Musk’s SpaceX is seeking permission from the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to dramatically increase activity at the Starbase facility. Previously, the company was allowed 25 launches and 50 landings a year, but now it is seeking permission for 456 launches and 912 landings annually.

Earlier this week, the US Federal Communications Commission granted SpaceX permission to send up to one million satellites into space as part of Musk’s plans to develop data centres in orbit.

articles.title: Man Keeps a Rock For Years, Hoping It's Gold. It Turned Out to Be So Much More Valuable
articles.summary: No wonder he couldn't crack it open!
articles.body:
In 2015, David Hole was prospecting in Maryborough Regional Park in central Victoria, Australia.

Armed with a metal detector, he discovered something out of the ordinary – a very heavy, reddish rock resting in some yellow clay.

He took it home and tried everything to open it, sure that there was a gold nugget inside the rock.

After all, Maryborough is in the Goldfields region, where the Australian gold rush peaked in the 19th century.

To break open his find, Hole tried a rock saw, an angle grinder, a drill, and even dousing it in acid. However, not even a sledgehammer could make a crack.

That's because what he was trying so hard to open was no gold nugget.

As he found out years later , it was a rare meteorite.

"It had this sculpted, dimpled look to it," Melbourne Museum geologist Dermot Henry told The Sydney Morning Herald in 2019.

"That's formed when they come through the atmosphere; they are melting on the outside, and the atmosphere sculpts them."

Unable to open the 'rock', but still intrigued, Hole took the nugget to the Melbourne Museum for identification.

"I've looked at a lot of rocks that people think are meteorites," Henry told Channel 10 News.

In fact, despite having worked at the museum for 37 years by that time and examining thousands of rocks, Henry said only two of the offerings had ever turned out to be real meteorites.

"If you saw a rock on Earth like this, and you picked it up, it shouldn't be that heavy," Melbourne Museum geologist Bill Birch, who is now curator emeritus, explained to The Sydney Morning Herald .

The researchers published a scientific paper in Proceedings of the Royal Society of Victoria , describing the 4.6 billion-year-old meteorite, which they called Maryborough after the town near where it was found.

"In some meteorites, there is 'stardust' even older than our Solar System." – geologist Dermot Henry

The Maryborough meteorite weighs a whopping 17 kilograms (37.5 pounds).

After researchers used a diamond saw to cut off a small slice, they found its composition had a high percentage of iron, making it an H5 ordinary chondrite .

Once opened, you can also see the tiny crystallized droplets of silicate minerals throughout it, called chondrules .

"Meteorites provide the cheapest form of space exploration . They transport us back in time, providing clues to the age, formation, and chemistry of our Solar System (including Earth)," said Henry.

"Some provide a glimpse at the deep interior of our planet. In some meteorites, there is 'stardust' even older than our Solar System, which shows us how stars form and evolve to create elements of the periodic table.

"Other rare meteorites contain organic molecules such as amino acids; the building blocks of life."

Although the researchers don't yet know where the meteorite came from and how long it may have been on Earth , they do have some guesses.

Our Solar System was once a spinning pile of dust and chondrite rocks.

Eventually gravity pulled a lot of this material together into planets, but the leftovers mostly ended up in a huge asteroid belt.

"This particular meteorite most probably comes out of the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and it's been nudged out of there by some asteroids smashing into each other, then one day it smashes into Earth ," Henry told Channel 10 News.

Carbon dating suggests the meteorite has been on Earth for less than 1,000 years, and there have been a number of meteor sightings between 1889 and 1951 that could correspond to its arrival on our planet .

The researchers argue that the Maryborough meteorite is much rarer than gold , making it far more valuable to science .

It's one of only 17 meteorites ever recorded in the Australian state of Victoria , and it's the second-largest chondritic mass, after a huge 55-kilogram specimen identified in 2003.

"This is only the 17th meteorite found in Victoria, whereas there's been thousands of gold nuggets found," Henry told Channel 10 News.

"Looking at the chain of events, it's quite, you might say, astronomical it being discovered at all."

It's not even the first meteorite to take a few years to make it to a museum.

In a particularly amazing story ScienceAlert covered in 2018, one space rock took 80 years, two owners, and a stint as a doorstop before finally being revealed for what it truly was.

Until recently, only a small fraction of meteorites that land on Earth had been firmly linked back to their parent body out in space.

But in 2024, three newly published papers gave us compelling origin stories for more than 90 percent of meteorites today.

Now is probably as good a time as any to check your backyard for particularly heavy and hard-to-break rocks – you might be sitting on a metaphorical gold mine .

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society of Victoria .

articles.title: Archaeologists found 28 ancient Gallic coins buried in a small pit beside human skull fragments and a five-centimetre bronze wagon wheel in northeastern France, raising the possibility of a long-lost sanctuary
articles.summary: Archaeologists working in northeastern France have uncovered 28 ancient Gallic coins in a small pit beside fragments of a human skull and a miniature
articles.body: Archaeologists working in northeastern France have uncovered 28 ancient Gallic coins in a small pit beside fragments of a human skull and a miniature bronze wagon wheel, a combination that suggests the site may have been a Late Iron Age sanctuary. The finds were made during preventive excavations near Bure in the Meuse department, an area being investigated in connection with France’s Cigéo deep geological repository project, as per reports by Inkorr and The History Blog.The discovery is significant because the objects appear to have been deliberately deposited rather than casually lost. The coins, known as potins, were found alongside human bone fragments and a five-centimetre metal wheel, a type of miniature object often associated with votive offerings in Iron Age Gaul. Researchers believe the site may have served a ritual purpose for the Leuci, a Gallic people who lived in the region during the Late La Tène period. Read more about it, as per the reports, here:What was foundThe excavation revealed a building measuring about 7.5 by 5.5 metres. Archaeologists identified four large postholes, each roughly one metre in diameter and more than 80 centimetres deep. The arrangement suggests that the posts may have leaned inward, possibly forming a conical structure rather than a conventional rectangular building.Inside one of the postholes, researchers recovered fragments of a human skull and lower jaw. The presence of human remains in an Iron Age sanctuary is not necessarily evidence of a burial in the modern sense. In ancient Gaul, skulls and other human remains could be treated as sacred deposits, particularly in ritual or ceremonial settings.The 28 cast Gallic coins were found in a small pit near the remains. These potins circulated in northeastern Gaul during the Late Iron Age and typically carried stylized imagery rather than realistic portraits. Their presence with skull fragments and a miniature wheel makes the assemblage especially unusual for the territory of the Leuci.The coins and the wheelThe coins depict a stylized human head influenced by portraits of Philip II of Macedon, along with a military standard shaped like a boar and a symbol resembling either a fleur-de-lis or an inverted letter T. Such imagery reflects the cultural connections and artistic influences circulating across Gaul in the centuries before Roman conquest.The miniature wheel is only about five centimetres wide. Archaeologists believe objects of this kind may have served as amulets or ritual offerings. At first glance, a wagon wheel doesn’t seem like an obvious religious symbol, but wheels were important in Iron Age societies both practically and symbolically. Vehicles, movement and the cycles of life could all have potent associations.The coins, wheel and human remains together form a pattern that is consistent with known votive practices. Many Iron Age sanctuaries contain pits, postholes or other defined spaces into which people deposited valuable or meaningful objects. The act of burial itself may have been part of the ritual, rather than simply a way of storing items.Why a sanctuary is likelyThe building’s unusual shape, the deliberate placement of objects, and the presence of human remains all support the idea that the site was more than an ordinary settlement structure. The large postholes suggest a substantial construction, while the small pit containing the coins and bone fragments points to a focused ritual deposit.Archaeologists cannot yet say exactly what ceremonies took place there or which deity, if any, was honoured. The evidence does, however, fit the broader pattern of Late Iron Age religious activity in Gaul, where sanctuaries often combined architecture, offerings, and symbolic deposits. The discovery is described as exceptionally rare for this part of the Leuci territory and unusual in Belgic Gaul more broadly.The term “sanctuary” does not necessarily mean a temple in the classical Roman sense. It can refer to a sacred space used for offerings, ceremonies, or communal rituals. The building may have housed such activities, while the deposits preserved in its postholes may represent offerings made at particular moments in the site’s use.A window into the LeuciThe Leuci were one of the Gallic peoples inhabiting parts of northeastern Gaul before Roman expansion reshaped the region. Finds like these help researchers understand not only what they made and used, but also how they organised belief, memory, and community life. Coins, for example, can reveal trade links, political imagery, and the movement of ideas across tribal boundaries.The skull fragments add an even creepier element. Human remains found in ritual context could reveal ancestor veneration, commemoration, trophy practices, or other customs that are hard to interpret from archeology alone. The bones will need further analysis by scientists to establish their age, sex, condition and whether they show any signs of trauma or deliberate treatment.The little wheel might be especially telling. If it was made specifically as an offering, rather than broken from a full-size vehicle, it strengthens the case that the deposit was ritual in nature. Its tiny size and careful positioning beside the coins and skull fragments suggests it was deliberately placed, and not accidentally lost.Why the site mattersThe discovery adds to a growing picture of religious and cultural life in Late Iron Age Gaul. It also shows how modern infrastructure projects can uncover evidence that would otherwise remain hidden beneath farmland, roads, and development sites. The excavation was carried out by France’s National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research, known as Inrap, as part of work linked to the Cigéo project.The area around Bure has already produced important archaeological finds, including burials with horses, gold and silver jewellery, and weapons dating to around 1,500 years ago. Some skeletons show potentially fatal weapon injuries, offering evidence of conflict during the decline of the Roman Empire. The new sanctuary discovery adds an earlier layer to that story, reaching back to the centuries before Roman rule.For now, the site remains under study. Further study of the coins, bones, soil and building remains could help archeologists develop a clearer chronology, and also learn if the structure was a sanctuary, a ritual enclosure or something more complex. What is already clear is that the small pit beside a human skull held more than loose change. It held a rare window into the beliefs and practices of ancient Gaul.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: More than 500 years after a Danish king's flagship exploded and sank off Sweden in 1495, divers found fine medieval chain-mail armour near a weapons chest, reopening questions about soldiers aboard the ship
articles.summary: More than five centuries after a Danish royal warship sank in the Baltic Sea, underwater archaeologists have discovered exceptionally well-preserved
articles.body: More than five centuries after a Danish royal warship sank in the Baltic Sea, underwater archaeologists have discovered exceptionally well-preserved fragments of medieval chain-mail armour near an ammunition-tool chest. The discovery could offer new clues about the soldiers and military equipment carried aboard the vessel before it exploded and sank off Sweden in 1495.The discovery was announced by the University of Southampton in a November 24, 2026, research update. An international team from the University of Southampton, Södertörn University and Stockholm University found the armour while investigating the wreck of Griffin, also known as Gribshunden, the 15th-century flagship of Danish King Hans. Researchers believe the area may have served as a storage space for military equipment, although its exact purpose remains uncertain.Armour discovered near an ammunition chestAccording to the University of Southampton, the researchers were examining the ship's superstructure, particularly its forecastle, an elevated fighting platform at the front of the vessel. While documenting an ammunition-tool chest, they discovered exposed fragments of fine copper-alloy chain mail nearby. The location is significant because the area beneath the forecastle may have been used to store military equipment. Researchers also collected samples of lead and other materials from the chest for further examination.Dr Rodrigo Pacheco-Ruiz, a visiting fellow at the University of Southampton's Centre for Maritime Archaeology and co-investigator on the Griffin project, said historical records indicated that German mercenaries, known as Landsknechts, were aboard the ship when it sank. The newly discovered armour may therefore have been associated with these soldiers and their equipment. However, researchers have not yet established the precise function of the storage area or identified who owned the chain mail.What the chain mail reveals about medieval soldiersThe quality of the armour has attracted particular attention, but researchers caution against assuming that it belonged to a wealthy knight or high-ranking individual. Rolf Fabricius Warming, a Southampton alumnus and doctoral researcher at Stockholm University who leads the project alongside Professor Johan Rönnby of Södertörn University, explained that high-quality chain mail could remain in use for extended periods.Soldiers often repaired and reused their armour rather than replacing it. The fragments could therefore represent older military equipment that remained in service when Griffin sank. Specialist analysis of the armour's manufacturing techniques and material composition could help researchers establish where it originated.The ammunition-tool chest is another important part of the investigation. Earlier expeditions had identified lead objects that might have been connected to ammunition moulds, although their precise purpose remains uncertain. By analysing the newly collected samples, researchers hope to understand how weapons and ammunition were manufactured, stored and supplied aboard the vessel.Danish king's flagship sank in 1495Griffin was the royal warship of King Hans of Denmark. The vessel also served diplomatic purposes, travelling to England in 1493 as part of an expedition carrying representatives of the monarch. In 1495, the ship was anchored north of Stora Ekö Island off the Swedish coast when an explosion caused it to catch fire and sink. King Hans was not aboard when the disaster occurred.The wreck was rediscovered by divers in the 1970s and has since become an important archaeological site. Its remarkably preserved condition offers researchers an opportunity to investigate late medieval shipbuilding, naval warfare and maritime technology. The Baltic Sea's low salinity has helped protect the wooden wreck from shipworms, which damage submerged timber in many other marine environments.Advanced technology helps researchers examine the wreckThe latest investigation combines traditional underwater archaeology with robotic seabed mapping and high-resolution three-dimensional imaging. Researchers used an uncrewed surface vehicle to survey the seabed while divers documented the ship's structure and archaeological remains. Photogrammetry, which creates detailed three-dimensional images from photographs, helped record the wreck and place the discoveries in their wider context.The international team hopes that examining the forecastle and its surrounding features will reveal how weapons, armour and military personnel were accommodated aboard the warship. In an interview with Live Science, Rolf Fabricius Warming said the researchers also hope to establish whether German mercenaries brought their own ammunition and tools aboard or received them from the Danish royal fleet.Further analysis of the chain mail and ammunition-tool chest may provide clues about the equipment, its origins and the organisation of military forces aboard one of Europe's important late medieval royal ships.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Australian scientists borrowed a marketing trick to lure invasive rats into trap-like tunnels: peanut butter was placed in an unreachable container outside, and entry rates for tunnels with bread rose by 83%
articles.summary: Marketing strategies work on the psychology of humans, they lure people into buying products they might not need, by slight manipulations.
articles.body: Marketing strategies work on the psychology of humans, they lure people into buying products they might not need, by slight manipulations. While aggressive marketing focuses on gaining visibility and retention in consumers’ minds, a high pressure marketing strategy used generally by telemarketers focuses on urgency. We would imagine that these strategies only work well on humans as greed and pleasure are inherently human qualities. Yet, rats in Australia have proven that even they are not immune to clever marketing.Researchers at the University of Sydney successfully trapped black rats (Rattus rattus) by applying a commonly used marketing tactic. The study can prove helpful in future efforts for wildlife detection and pest control.An age old problemBlack rats (Rattus rattus) are believed to have arrived with the first European settlers, and they've made themselves at home along coastal Australia ever since. They are an invasive species, which basically implies that they breed in large quantities and eat or outcompete native wildlife.Humans have been trying to outsmart them for centuries, and the usual playbook is better bait and deadlier traps. But there's a catch that anyone who has ever set a trap in the garage will recognise: the rat has to actually go in. Wary, clever and perfectly happy with their current snack, plenty of rats simply don't.Enter the nudgeA team at the University of Sydney, led by Professor Peter Banks and Senior Research Officer Jenna Bytheway, decided to stop asking "how do we make the bait better?" and started focusing on being more clever than the rats.Their idea was based on “nudge” marketing. It is where businesses use tricks to increase the appeal of options you are more likely to prefer. You know the feeling. You're scrolling through an online shop, and the jumper you've been eyeing says "Sold Out." Suddenly you want it more than anything, and the available alternatives look a little dull by comparison.Professor Banks has framed the idea as altering what an animal thinks it's missing out on rather than what it stands to gain. That is a clever reversal in a field that has mostly focused on making rewards bigger.The experimentOver two years, the researchers set up hundreds of small trap-like tunnels across urban bushland in Sydney. There were infrared, motion-sensing cameras watching each trap, so the team could see how free-living black rats responded to the baits.Inside the tunnels went a range of baits, including strawberry jam sandwiches, plain white bread, or nothing at all. But, among them, half the tunnels had a setup of peanut butter bait balls which were put inside steel shakers and placed at the entrances of the tunnels. As described by the Univerity, they acted as phantom decoys which are a kind of information decoy that consists of highly desirable but inaccessible food. So, the rats could smell the irresistible stuff, but they couldn't get at it.It's the rodent equivalent of walking past a bakery window, nose pressed to the glass, then being offered a slice of plain bread instead. And apparently, the bread suddenly looks pretty good.What did the researchers findThe results were published in the Journal of Applied Ecology with the title, ‘Information decoys improve animal engagement with management devices.’ The results were striking. When the decoy sat outside a tunnel baited with low-quality plain bread, rat entries jumped by 83 per cent. Rats were also 2.7 times more likely to walk into a bread tunnel when the decoy was there.Noticeably, interactions didn’t boost when peanut butter was used as bait inside the tunnel. So, while the rats love peanut butter, it might not be the best thing to trap the rats. It is the tease for the unreachable treat that changed the rats' sense of what they might be losing.You can even watch the footage the team released, which shows how rats behave with and without the decoy at the entrance.Why this matters beyond ratsIt might sound like a quirky lab curiosity, but the practical payoff could be significant. Conservation work depends on animals actually engaging with the devices set out for them, whether that's traps, tracking tunnels or poison bait stations. The team told University of Sydney that phantom decoys could help most in two situations: when bait alone isn't attractive enough, and in the final stages of a control operation, when the last few stubborn animals are the hardest to detect or catch.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Weeks before Democrat governor Gina Hinojosa takes office, Texas grants permit to SpaceX's $24 billion Boca Chica gas power plant; as the 'now Blue state' resumes …
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s SpaceX has secured an air pollution permit from Texas for a natural gas power plant at Boca Chica, weeks before Democratic Governor-elect Gina
articles.body: Elon Musk’s SpaceX has secured an air pollution permit from Texas for a natural gas power plant at Boca Chica, weeks before Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa takes office. The plant is part of a proposed supercomputing complex east of Brownsville. The city of Starbase estimates that the initial phases of the power plant and computing facility will cost about $24 billion.The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued three air permits last week after lifting a pause on permits for data center projects. Besides SpaceX, the approvals covered a power plant that would supply CloudBurst’s data center near San Marcos and an Atlas Energy Solutions plant northeast of Abilene. Before issuing the permits, outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott’s office told the agency that the state’s grid operator had finished gathering information on how data centers could affect local communities.What Gina Hinojosa has promised on data centersThe permits give developers an opening before Texas lawmakers return in January. Hinojosa, the first Democrat elected Texas governor since 1990, campaigned on pausing new data center development, ending tax breaks for the industry and giving local communities more say over where projects are built. Abbott had already moved to tighten oversight before the election, calling on developers to cover their own costs, secure their own water supplies and protect the power grid.SpaceX still has a local decision ahead. Starbase commissioners are scheduled to hold a public hearing on December 9 on a proposed property tax break for the project, which would occupy about 444 acres near the Port of Brownsville.Why data center developers are building their own power plantsLong waits for grid connections are one reason developers are turning to on-site generation. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas was weighing more than 474 gigawatts of connection requests in August. By September, 204 projects totalling 66.4 gigawatts had provisionally qualified to move forward with their initial power requests. Another 158 projects, representing 127.9 gigawatts, qualified for further study and could face longer waits or receive less power than requested.Texas accounts for nearly half the roughly 90 gigawatts of planned capacity across 59 US data centers looking to generate their own power, according to Cleanview data cited by the Financial Times. The state’s natural gas supplies and pipeline network make that option attractive. But tighter rules could change where the next projects go. articles.title: Why does Elon Musk want to put a million satellite data centres in space?
articles.summary: The US FCC authorised the plan on Wednesday, calling it a first in the history of the country.
articles.body:
SpaceX founder and billionaire Elon Musk’s plan to launch a million satellites was approved this week by the United States, as controversy over data centres needed to drive the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution leads to a scramble for alternative locations.

On Wednesday, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) authorised the plan, named “Starmind”, and said it marks a first in the history of the country.

“At this pivotal time in America’s development of super intelligence [artificial intelligence], the FCC is granting SpaceX authorisation to deploy 1,000,000 orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth,” the FCC said in a statement posted on X by Chairman Brendan Carr.

Carr said under President Donald Trump’s leadership, the US was “moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers benefits for the American people”.

“This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership and expand prosperity here at home,” he said.

Here’s everything we know about the plan to send a million satellites to space:

With data centres being the crucial backbone behind AI computing, and with demand for the software rapidly growing, Musk’s plan provides an alternative: Using the sun as a power source for them.

According to SpaceX, which manufactures rockets and spacecraft, the new project works by using “satellites with localised AI compute, where the results are beamed back from [a] low-latency, sun-synchronous orbit”.

This, SpaceX claims, is “the fastest way to scale given the growing difficulty of finding electrical power sources on Earth”.

On its website, SpaceX calls the plan “low-cost [and] high performance”.

But Musk’s company already has satellites in space, with Starmind only expected to add to the constellation.

According to SatFleet Live, which tracks satellites in real time, there are 16,928 active satellites in orbit now. Of that, 11,190 (66 percent) are SpaceX Starlink satellites, the company’s internet outfit.

Under the FCC’s licence, SpaceX must begin its deployment of the satellite data centres no later than November 2033; send 10 percent of the maximum number, 100,000, no later than November 2035 in the same month; deploy 50 percent to space by November 2038 and the whole constellation by 2040.

Why does Musk want to send them up, and what’s the advantage?

As AI scales up rapidly, the need for data centres grows.

But data centres need vast tracts of land, and guzzle water and power, while churning out tonnes of fossil fuel emissions. They generate intense heat, and cooling systems need large amounts of water to keep the technology running, putting pressure on water supplies and communities facing drought, especially as climate change raises global temperatures.

According to an article published by the Environmental and Energy Study Institute, a US nonprofit, in 2025, “large data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons per day, equivalent to the water use of a town populated by 10,000 to 50,000 people.”

These concerns have set off mass protests against data centres, from the US to Kenya to India. Widespread opposition to data centres was a key issue for many voters in the US midterm elections earlier this month, per polling data.

In July, demonstrators against the rapid expansion of data centres held 142 protests across 42 states in a nationwide effort against AI infrastructure expansion.

Satellite-based data centres face no similar land constraints, and they can, in theory, use solar power – as SpaceX says is the plan – to fuel their processing. But cooling in space remains a challenge: Unlike on Earth, there is no air or water, so heat released can’t escape via conduction or convection.

Astronomers and environmentalists have criticised the plan, saying it will amplify sky pollution that makes it harder to see the night sky.

On Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s approval of the plan.

“As the AAS stated in its earlier filings to the FCC, the proposed constellation would significantly undermine (i) decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and (ii) the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” the statement read.

“The AAS is gravely concerned about the future of federally funded astronomical research under such a fundamentally altered night sky, and the resulting waste of taxpayer dollars invested in astronomical facilities throughout the country and the world,” it said. “While we hope that SpaceX will continue to coordinate with the National Science Foundation, we remain concerned by the lack of formal coordination requirements in the license granted to SpaceX in this case.”
