articles.title: Tube strike ends but more dates set for December
articles.summary: More industrial action by the RMT is planned for December, January and February.
articles.body:
The first in a series of 24-hour strikes on the London Underground has ended, with more industrial action planned for December, January and February.

Tube drivers from the Rail, Maritime and Transport (RMT) union walked out at noon on Thursday, with workers ending their action at noon on Friday.

The strike action was the result of a dispute between the union and Transport for London (TfL) over the changing terms and conditions attached to the option of a four or five day week.

On Friday, six Underground lines were suspended or part-suspended, and five others experienced delays. Disruption was forecast to last until 18:00 GMT "as services start to recover".

Simon Mitchell, chief executive at hospitality organisation Kerb, said the Tube strike could not have come "at a worse time" for businesses.

Kerb operates Seven Dials Market in Covent Garden in London's West End.

Mitchell told BBC London there was a "big drop" in footfall on Thursday and he anticipated the same on Friday.

It came at a "really hard time for all hospitality businesses", he said, adding that although the strike was for 24 hours, it had affected two trading days.

He said the upcoming strikes in December were "planned for the best week of trading in the whole of Christmas and what would be our best week of the whole year".

He urged the RMT to call off the strike, adding "we're on our knees".

TfL said the number of Tube drivers who booked on for their shift during the strike was higher than during previous industrial action, and more than 55% of the Tube network ran on Thursday.

Although there was disruption across the network as anticipated on Friday morning, the Jubilee and Victoria lines were able to start at the normal time and all lines were operating services before 06:30 GMT, earlier than expected, TfL said.

Despite a limited Piccadilly service and no service on the Waterloo & City line lowering the average, the network was said to be operating just over 40% of services on Friday morning up to 09:00.

On Thursday, usage across the transport network was at 90% of normal levels, with Tube ridership at around two thirds of normal levels.

Forest, which operates e-bikes in London, said it experienced a 17% increase in rides on Thursday evening compared to the same time last week.

Uber said it also saw an increase in demand as a result of the strike action.

Two trade unions represent London Underground train drivers: Aslef and the RMT.

During the strike on Thursday and Friday, only RMT members walked out, as Aslef has agreed to TfL's voluntary compressed four-day week and previously said it was "surprised that the RMT has decided to take this action".

Aslef primarily represents Tube train drivers, while the RMT represents drivers as well as general operational, engineering, maintenance and station workers.

The dispute follows the introduction by TfL of a new framework for drivers, who have been given the option of a four or five-day week.

The RMT said it supported the framework but did not agree with changing workers' existing terms and conditions.

The union also expressed concern that staying on the old deal would lead to working practice changes including moving depots.

General secretary Eddie Dempsey has said: "RMT is not opposed to a genuine four-day working week that benefits our members, but we will not accept it being used as a vehicle for job cuts, intensified working and the erosion of terms and conditions."

TfL said changes to working patterns were voluntary. A spokesperson said: "Any suggestion otherwise is misleading the public in order to justify strike action over proposals that would give Tube drivers more time off and create a more modern, efficient Tube service."

On Friday morning, some commuters faced being late for work and missed appointments.

At King's Cross, the reduced service TfL ran through the station coped with demand and no platforms were packed with passengers waiting for delayed Tube trains.

Ollie, a stall trader outside King's Cross, said the walkout had left trade "really slow" as fewer people travelled in and spent money at stalls.

With Christmas approaching, he said it was a vital time for traders to earn money as more visitors came to London's Christmas markets.

He said: "I think holding Tube strikes like so often is a bit excessive and I don't think there's really any need for it."

This was echoed by Amelia, who works at The Flower Station bakery stall outside King's Cross station.

"I think it affects a lot more people than they realise," she said of the strike. "I appreciate that they obviously have their reasons for striking, but it impacts a lot more people than they think - not just people getting to and from work, but businesses like us."

In Finsbury Park, people could be seen running for buses and trying to board the few Tube services that were running.

One young woman waiting for the bus said that she was concerned she would miss her A-level mock exam.

"I'm just stressed out, I need to get to school immediately. I need to get the bus but they aren't working, so I'm just standing here," Aya told BBC London.

"I'm going to be late so I'll have to explain it to the teachers, but hopefully they'll understand."

Marie, who was also at Finsbury Park, said she had been left "waiting for buses that don't show up".

She was trying to get home with her guinea pigs after collecting them from a sitter after returning from a trip to Morocco.

She said she used a Lime bike to travel to the sitter, but wanted to use a bus to travel home with her pets.

The strike "makes life really complicated and stressful", she said.

Asked for her reaction to the seven remaining strikes planned over the coming months, Marie said it "just complicates our lives".

It went beyond getting into the office for work, she said, adding that it was "almost impossible" for her to travel across London to see friends when strikes were on.

articles.title: SpaceX stock rises after Musk pledges annual share giveaway for kids
articles.summary: SpaceX stock rose after Elon Musk expanded his share pledge for US children.
articles.body:
SpaceX ( SPCX ) stock rose about 3% Friday after CEO Elon Musk said on X Thursday that he would give "all kids in America" another share of the company each year.

On Wednesday, Musk, who also runs Tesla ( TSLA ), had previously promised that "every child in America" would receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from him. SpaceX said its gift would go to currently active Trump Accounts and that Musk would match it. Musk didn't say whether his annual giveaway would follow the same eligibility rules.

Trump Accounts are available to eligible minors with a Social Security number. The 2025–2028 birth window applies to the federal government's one-time $1,000 contribution.

SpaceX shares were trading about 12% below their $150 opening trade in June as of Friday morning. The stock has come under pressure amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks and concerns that a potential merger with Tesla ( TSLA ) could dilute SpaceX shareholders.

SpaceX's AI division, which it calls Super Intelligence, accounted for just over half of the company's revenue and more than 80% of its capital spending in the third quarter.

articles.title: A study of 226 mothers with children aged 2 to 6 found that mothers of three or more children were less accepting of their young children's anger than mothers of one or two, even after accounting for stress
articles.summary: Children have a rather interesting way of showing that they are angry. More than our own angry parents, we sometimes dread an angry child.
articles.body: Children have a rather interesting way of showing that they are angry. More than our own angry parents, we sometimes dread an angry child. A toy they cannot have, food they do not like, or even simply being told no can turn into a full-blown tantrum within seconds. For adults, these outbursts may seem unnecessary or even frustrating, but for a young child, they are often one of the few ways of expressing emotions they have not yet learnt to understand. And it is the responsibility of parents to teach their kids how to manage these feelings.But what happens to the child when parents themselves run out of patience? That is something the recent study explores. Being born is not something kids decide; it is the decision of the parents to have children, and each child, by that logic, deserves the same amount of love and patience. But what if even mothers' love has a saturation point?A recent study published titled The unique effect of the number of children on mothers’ acceptance of children’s negative emotions in the journal Cognition and Emotion has explored this relationship, examining whether the number of children a mother has influences how accepting she is of her young child's negative emotions. The findings offer an interesting perspective on how family size may shape the way mothers respond to childhood anger and frustration.What the study found about mothers of larger familiesTo understand this relationship, researchers surveyed 226 mothers in Portugal who had at least one child between the ages of two and six. They looked at how mothers perceived and responded to different negative emotions expressed by their young children, particularly anger, sadness and fear. The aim was to understand whether the number of children in a family had any connection with how acceptable mothers found these emotional expressions.The findings showed a noticeable difference among mothers based on family size. Those raising three or more children were less accepting of their young children's expressions of anger and frustration than mothers with one or two children. Interestingly, this difference remained even after the researchers accounted for factors such as parenting stress and mindful parenting, so parenting stress alone cannot be blamed.But what makes the finding particularly interesting is that this pattern was not observed across every negative emotion. The number of children a mother had was associated with her acceptance of anger and frustration, but not in the same way with her acceptance of emotions such as sadness and fear. This suggests that the challenge may not be with negative emotions as a whole, but with the more outward expressions of displeasure that can sometimes make parenting difficult.Why mothers may find it harder to accept anger in larger familiesRaising a child requires patience, but raising several children also means navigating different personalities, needs and emotions under the same roof. With each child having their own needs and a different version of you to attend to, it might make the day a little frustrating. A parent may have to attend to one child's needs while managing another's tantrum, resolving disagreements between siblings or simply keeping up with the everyday demands of the household. In such an environment, a child's anger may become another emotional demand that a mother has to respond to, sometimes leaving her with less room to accommodate an outburst.Anger is a particularly difficult emotion to handle because it often gets expressed more visibly than other emotions. A young child may shout, resist instructions, throw things or become upset when they do not get what they want. While these reactions are a part of emotional development, they can test a parent's patience, particularly when several children require attention at the same time.However, it is important to understand that the study does not establish that mothers with larger families are necessarily less patient or less loving, or that having more children directly causes this difference. It just shows an association between family size and mothers' acceptance of childhood anger, leaving room for further research into the reasons behind it.And at the end of the day, mothers are human too. They have their own limits, frustrations, responsibilities and difficult days, and expecting them to respond with endless patience to every situation is hardly realistic. But a child is not responsible for the decision to bring them into the world, nor should they have to bear the consequences of an adult's exhaustion simply for expressing emotions they are still learning to understand. Every child deserves to feel that their emotions have a place in the family, even when those emotions are difficult to deal with. Understanding a mother's limitations should not mean overlooking a child's emotional needs. Both deserve empathy, and parenting must leave room for both.Fearless legend or grounded realist?
